Andrew Jackson. The seventh President of the United States and the dominant political figure of the eighteen twenties and thirties, Jackson was a military hero and populist outsider who reshaped the presidency and the Democratic Party by championing the common man against the elite.

His military fame rested on his victory at the Battle of New Orleans in eighteen fifteen during the War of eighteen twelve. He became a national hero and the symbol of American frontier individualism. Elected president in eighteen twenty-eight after the controversial election of eighteen twenty-four, in which he lost to John Quincy Adams despite winning a plurality of votes. Adams's appointment as secretary of state to Henry Clay sparked the "Corrupt Bargain" narrative that fueled Jackson's populist challenge.

Jackson championed Jacksonian Democracy—the belief that power should flow to ordinary citizens and that the federal government's elites were corrupt. Mass participation in politics surged during his era. He signed the Indian Removal Act in eighteen thirty, which forced thousands of Native Americans, particularly the Cherokees, Creeks, and Seminoles, westward on the Trail of Tears. This was one of the darkest chapters in American history, resulting in thousands of deaths.

Jackson clashed with South Carolina over the Nullification Crisis from eighteen thirty-two to eighteen thirty-three. The state refused to enforce federal tariff laws, claiming states had the right to nullify federal laws. Jackson's firm response asserted federal supremacy but heightened sectional tensions. He dismantled the Second Bank of the United States by vetoing its recharter in eighteen thirty-two and removing federal deposits. Populist anti-bank sentiment drove this action, though the move destabilized the economy. He pioneered the spoils system, rewarding political supporters with government jobs, which corrupted the civil service but cemented party loyalty as a political principle.
